t: Maximum Hamming Distances — Multi-Source BFS on the Hypercube
o: All values live in the m-dimensional hypercube (m ≤ 17, so ≤ 131072 nodes) where edges flip one bit and graph distance equals Hamming distance. For each nums[i], the farthest array element is found by computing, for the **complement** of nums[i], the distance to the nearest array element: answer[i] = m − d(comp(nums[i])). Compute d(·) for all 2^m nodes once via multi-source BFS seeded from every value in nums. Example: nums=[9,12,9,11], comp(9)=0110; nearest seed 1011 differs in 1 bit → answer 4−1=3… wait, for 9 the expected answer is 2 — nearest seed to 0110 is 1100 (distance 2) → 4−2=2. Correct.
k: Hamming distance = shortest-path distance on the m-cube.
max Hamming from v to the set = m − min Hamming from ~v to the set.

a.n: Approach 1: Multi-source BFS from all nums values
a.i: Seed the BFS with every nums value (dist 0), expand by flipping single bits; dist[x] = min Hamming distance from x to the set. Each answer is m − dist[complement].
s: Build dist array of size 2^m, init ∞; enqueue all nums values with dist 0.
a.t: O(2^m · m) — each cube node processed once with m neighbors

a.n: Approach 2: Iterative relaxation (BFS by levels without queue)
a.i: Since edge weights are uniform, repeatedly relax all nodes m times (like Bellman-Ford on the cube): dist_new[v] = min over bits of dist[u^bit]+1. Simpler to write, same asymptotics with a larger constant.
s: Repeat m rounds: for every node, relax against all single-bit neighbors.
a.t: O(2^m · m²) — m relaxation rounds over all nodes and bits

w: The complement trick is the crux — brute-forcing all pairs is O(n²·m) and too slow at n = 2^m. Note duplicates in nums are harmless (dedupe seeds implicitly). Follow-up: SOHA-style subset-sum-over-bits DP achieves the same with dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[v^bit]+1) in-place per bit.
